transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Dr. Aaron Patel (CTO - Northbridge), Samantha Lee (ML Eng - Northbridge), Daniel Kim (Head of Product - Northbridge)

Summary (auto): Redwood shows model catalog, benchmark views, and compatibility matrix. Discussed open models, quantization, latency/cost tradeoffs, and private deployment options for PHI. Agreed next steps to run pilot benchmarks and share security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya Chen, AE at Redwood. With me is Liam, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:30] Dr. Patel: Good, thanks. We've been excited to see the model catalog — we're trying to pick an open model for our patient triage assistant. Main things: latency, cost, and HIPAA compliance.
[01:15] Maya: Perfect, that's exactly what we'll cover. Quick agenda: model selection walkthrough in the catalog, demo of benchmarks and cost signals, then the compatibility matrix for deploying hosted/dedicated/private.
[02:00] Liam: I'll jump into the console in a sec, but high level — we surface curated open models and verified perf profiles. We also show quantization recommendations and hardware compatibility per model.
[02:45] Samantha: Quick Q — when you say "verified perf profiles" is that measured on your infra or on cloud provider VMs?
[03:10] Liam: Good question. It's measured end-to-end on Redwood's runtime across representative hardware types; we also publish the kernel/quantization settings used. There can be slight diffs on customer on-prem infra.
[03:45] Daniel: Also curious: can we filter models by token usage cost and sequence length? Our prompts are typically 100-250 tokens.
[04:20] Maya: Yes, filterable. In the catalog you can pick target latency threshold, token budget, and it surfaces likely candidates. Let's switch over to the console — Liam?
[04:50] Liam: Sure, sharing screen now. Sorry if the screen name shows my personal desktop — um, let me open the model catalog tab.
[05:30] Liam: So here's the catalog. At the top we tag models by family, parameter count, and recommended deployment. You can see open models like LlamaX-13B, Redmond-7B (internal shorthand), and GLaM-like variants. Note: some names in the UI are short-hand; actual model artifacts listed in the artifact column.
[06:10] Dr. Patel: I noticed LlamaX-13B name — is that the one with 4-bit quant recommended?
[06:35] Liam: For many 13B variants, our recommendation is 4-bit quant (Q4) on NVMe-backed nodes when you need better cost; we also have a Q8 path for lower latency. The compatibility matrix shows which quant levels are supported on which hardware.
[07:10] Samantha: How do we interpret the benchmark chart? There's p50/p95 and a separate token-cost column.
[07:40] Liam: Right. p50 is median latency to first token, p95 is tail — important for user experience. Token cost is estimated cost per 1M tokens under current runtime settings; these are estimates that include batching assumptions.
[08:15] Daniel: Do these benchmarks use your standard batching window? Our app needs low latency for interactive triage — want to keep p50 under 250ms.
[08:45] Liam: We show multiple benchmark slices: single-request (no batching), small batch (up to 4), and large batch. For interactive, look at single-request numbers. For example, on our A500-equivalent nodes LlamaX-13B Q8 p50 single-request was ~220ms in our tests.
[09:30] Maya: Note that if you need guaranteed p50 we recommend Dedicated with pinned nodes; we can supply throughput SLAs. Hosted is usually fine for early stages but Dedicated gives isolation and predictable tail latency.
[10:05] Dr. Patel: Can you run a pilot on our data? We want the benchmark with our prompts and some PHI redaction steps.
[10:35] Liam: Yep, we typically run a pilot: you send a small prompt set and we'll run it on 2-3 shortlisted models and report p50/p95 and token cost. For PHI we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with strict retention settings.
[11:10] Samantha: About Private: how does your KMS/HSM integration work? We have a corporate KMS and need key control.
[11:40] Maya: Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; we also support VPC peering and on-prem package for air-gapped needs. We'll share the security doc (SOC2, encryption, KMS mapping).
[12:15] Daniel: Any customers running inference on-prem with similar constraints?
[12:40] Liam: Yes, a few regulated health customers run Private or Dedicated. There are perf tradeoffs — on-prem hardware topology matters — we put that in the compatibility guide.
[13:10] Maya: Back to the catalog, you can click into a model to see the compatibility matrix — which quant levels, sequence length limits (e.g., 2048 vs 8192), and recommended instance families.
[13:45] Liam: I'll open LlamaX-13B detail. See here: supported quantizations Q4/Q8/Q16, recommended max seq 4096, estimated memory footprint per KV cache and recommended batch sizing.
[14:20] Samantha: Our use case sometimes needs longer context, sometimes not. If we pick a model limited to 4096 and later need 8192, how hard is switching?
[14:50] Liam: You can pin model versions and roll out a variant; switching to a longer context model typically means a different artifact or another config — doable but needs re-benchmarking for latency and cost.
[15:25] Dr. Patel: The compatibility matrix shows OS/gpu drivers — some of our infra is older CUDA. Is there guidance?
[15:55] Liam: Yes, we surface kernel requirements and minimum driver versions. For older setups we recommend Redwood-managed nodes or Dedicated where we ensure compatibility.
[16:30] Maya: Quick note about cost: our Optimize toolkit will suggest quantization and batching settings to reduce token cost while keeping latency SLOs. We'll show a quick example.
[17:05] Liam: Opening Optimize tab. Here you can run a "what-if" to compare models under target latency and token budgets. For instance, switching from 16-bit to Q4 can cut token compute cost ~2.5x but may impact perplexity; we flag models that degrade beyond a threshold.
[17:45] Daniel: How do you measure quality degradation? We have safety/accuracy requirements for triage — must not hallucinate clinical advice.
[18:15] Liam: We tie quality regressions to evals and prompt sets; you can upload your tests and we run automatic scoring (F1/EM or custom metrics). Optimize surfaces regression alerts and recommends alternate models or fallback policies.
[18:55] Samantha: Any automated fallback? Like if latency spikes, can you route to a smaller model?
[19:20] Liam: Yes, smart routing supports policy-based fallbacks — route to a cheaper smaller model or lower-cost region if latency or capacity drops. You can configure thresholds.
[19:55] Maya: Let's show the benchmark report for the shortlisted models: LlamaX-13B Q8, Redmond-7B Q4, and Falcon-ish-30B (we include a trimmed variant).
[20:30] Liam: Here's the chart: single-request p50/p95, token cost estimate, throughput. Note — the Falcon-ish-30B shows higher cost but better zero-shot on some prompts. Redmond-7B Q4 gives lowest cost and sub-200ms p50 on A500-equivalent.
[21:05] Dr. Patel: Those numbers look promising. How accurate are estimates for our real traffic distribution?
[21:35] Liam: They are estimates based on sampled request distributions; best practice is to run a pilot with your exact traffic. We'll run p50/p95 and cost using your prompt mix.
[22:00] Daniel: On deployment: if we start hosted and then move to Dedicated, is there a migration path?
[22:30] Maya: Yes, same API and model pinning; we can export rollout configs and migrate traffic with canary rollouts in the Console.
[23:05] Samantha: One more security question — audit logs: do you provide per-request logs and redaction policies?
[23:35] Liam: We provide request/response traces and token-level usage; for PHI we support configurable retention and redaction hooks. In Private, you can keep logs in your environment.
[24:10] Dr. Patel: Pricing: can you do a rough delta between hosted and Dedicated? We have 10M tokens/month baseline for the pilot, potential to scale.
[24:40] Maya: Hosted is pay-as-you-go; Dedicated has a monthly commit but lowers unit cost and gives SLAs. I'll send a quick pricing matrix after the call with both hosted e2e and Dedicated commit examples.
[25:15] Daniel: Competitors — we've also talked to OpenAI and Anthropic; they have good quality but we're looking for open model flexibility and lower cost.
[25:45] Liam: Right — we emphasize model choice and operational controls for rollouts and optimise cost. We also run our own verified benchmarks to compare.
[26:20] Maya: Ok, demo bit — I'm going to click into the benchmark detail and show the raw traces. You'll see per-request timing and the KV cache hit rates which matter for repeated prompts.
[26:55] Liam: Note the cache column — cold-start vs warmed KV cache changes latency significantly on long sessions. Optimize suggests prefix caching for repeated conversations.
[27:30] Samantha: For triage sessions we reuse some patient context across messages — prefix caching could help. How do we enable that?
[27:55] Liam: It's automatic for session-backed routes; you can also configure cache TTLs and size per model. For PHI we recommend TTL aligned with retention policy.
[28:30] Daniel: Any limitations around function calling or structured output? We rely on JSON outputs for extraction.
[28:55] Liam: We support structured output and function/tool calling; we also have an output schema tester in the Console to validate responses.
[29:30] Maya: I'll show the compatibility matrix PDF we attach — it lists kernel/driver/quant combos and recommended instance families.
[30:00] Liam: Scrolling — here, see hardware mapping: A500-equivalent (8x16GB) recommended for 13B Q8 interactive, H100-equivalent for large 30B workloads, and CPU fallback for small embedding tasks.
[30:40] Dr. Patel: We have some on-prem A500-class nodes; would that map cleanly?
[31:05] Liam: Likely yes, but we'll validate in the pilot. For on-prem with older drivers we might need driver updates.
[31:40] Samantha: Can you include the exact docker image or runtime hash? Our infra team needs that for approvals.
[32:05] Maya: Yes, we can share runtime images and hashes and the audit trail. We'll include that in the security pack.
[32:40] Daniel: How long does a typical pilot take and what are success metrics?
[33:05] Liam: Usually 1-2 weeks of run time for benchmark window; success metrics: p50/p95 under X, token cost below threshold, and no regressions on your eval suite. We'll propose a pilot plan.
[33:40] Dr. Patel: For cost calculations, do you include KV cache benefits in token cost?
[34:05] Liam: Yes, we can run 'warm' vs 'cold' scenarios and show adjusted token compute cost.
[34:40] Maya: I'm going to show the 'Model compare' export. You can download a CSV with per-model metrics, configuration used, and a compatibility summary.
[35:10] Samantha: That CSV will be helpful to share with procurement. Please include sequence length and recommended quant.
[35:45] Maya: We'll include it. Quick note on fallbacks again — you can set a route to try model A and if latency > 500ms auto-failover to model B.
[36:15] Daniel: How does billing work during a pilot? Is it pro-rated or waived?
[36:40] Maya: For early pilots we often give trial credits for the first run; for larger pilots we typically put a small committed amount or a short-term Dedicated. I'll outline options in the follow-up.
[37:10] Dr. Patel: Our security team will want a call. Can we get a security deep-dive?
[37:35] Maya: Absolutely — we usually do a 30-45 minute security review with our security lead and your security team. We'll schedule for week of 3/15 per earlier note.
[38:05] Liam: One more technical detail: the compatibility matrix lists max KV cache memory per model; for multi-tenant Dedicated we partition KV cache per route.
[38:40] Samantha: Any QA on hallucinations for medical content? We need guardrails.
[39:05] Liam: We recommend prompt engineering, eval tests, and a hybrid policy: rule-based checks plus model-level scoring. Optimize can surface regression on your evals and auto-alert.
[39:40] Daniel: Can we set up a canary route that logs responses for a week before full roll?
[40:05] Maya: Yes, canary rollouts with tracing hooks are supported. You can restrict sample rates and storage.
[40:40] Dr. Patel: For data residency, are there region locks? We operate in US-East and need logs kept in region.
[41:05] Liam: We support region pinning and data residency controls on Dedicated and Private. Hosted can be region-specific but ask in the follow-up for guarantees.
[41:40] Samantha: Anything else in the Optimize tooling that helps reduce costs mid-flight?
[42:05] Liam: Automatic batching policies, dynamic quantization suggestions, and cache strategies. Also scheduled off-peak bulk jobs moved to cheaper pools.
[42:40] Maya: Wrapping up — recap: we'll send model catalog CSV, pricing, security pack. Redwood will run pilot plan after sample prompts are shared.
[43:20] Dr. Patel: Great. Action items for us: Samantha will send sample prompts and expected traffic; Daniel will coordinate procurement timeline; I'll loop in security.
[43:50] Maya: Awesome. I'll send the follow-up email with attachments and proposed pilot dates.
[44:20] Samantha: Quick note — can you include an example compatibility matrix highlight for LlamaX-13B so our infra can pre-check drivers?
[44:45] Liam: Yep, will attach that.
[45:15] Daniel: Any required signatures for a pilot?
[45:35] Maya: Typically an MSA addendum or pilot agreement; we'll include a template. Procurement can sign digitally.
[46:05] Dr. Patel: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[46:25] Maya: Thanks all. We'll follow up.
[46:40] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcription includes a few shorthand names and occasional mis-hearings (e.g., Redmond-7B as shorthand); speaker labels approximate. Links shared during call: model catalog CSV export (link), security pack (link), pilot plan draft (link).
